content: Butternut canker is a disease caused by the fungus Sirococcus clavigignenti-juglandacearum, which specifically parasitizes members of the Juglandaceae family. This disease was first identified in Wisconsin in 1967 and has since spread to other regions, including Canada. Surveys have shown that the disease has severely impacted butternut tree populations, with 84% of butternut trees in Michigan and 58% in Wisconsin affected. In Virginia and North Carolina, the butternut population has declined drastically from 7.5 million to 2.5 million trees. Later studies revealed that 91% of all living butternut trees were either diseased or cankered. The symptoms of butternut canker include the development of elongated and broad cankers on the main stem, branches, young twigs, and exposed roots. In advanced stages, these cankers are often covered with bark cracks and shredded bark. The life cycle of the fungus begins with the release of pycnidiospores during rainy periods. These spores infect the tree by entering through wounds or broken branches, where they germinate and penetrate deeply into the tree tissues, forming cankers. The infection hyphae primarily invade the parenchyma phloem intracellularly, but they can also spread intercellularly through uniseriate and multiseriate xylem ray cells and parenchyma cells. Over time, the fungus produces mycelial mats of stroma and mycelial pegs. The stroma mats generate unior multilocular pycnidia, which contain branched and unbranched conidiophores that produce two-celled pycnidiospores. These spores are eventually ejected through the pycnidial ostiole. These pegs also produce smaller pycnidia compared to those in the stroma, but the spores they release are identical. Resistance to butternut canker varies among tree species. Heartnut and Japanese walnut trees exhibit the highest levels of resistance. These trees possess periderm layers that are 35-45 cells thick, which act as a physical barrier to fungal penetration. Furthermore, they produce phenolic compounds immediately upon fungal attack, followed by the production of gums and tyloses to encapsulate the pathogen. Other species, such as butternut, black walnut, and Persian walnut, show varying degrees of resistance. Historically, the removal of infected trees was recommended to prevent the spread of the disease. However, this approach is now considered less effective, as the disease has become widespread across the entire range of butternut trees. Moreover, removing infected trees may inadvertently eliminate those that exhibit partial resistance to the fungus, thereby reducing the potential for developing resistant progeny. There are documented cases of long-term survival in pure butternut trees infected with the canker, suggesting that some level of resistance exists within the population. Recent findings indicate that the fungus can be internally seed-borne, necessitating strict quarantine protocols for seeds, especially when they are intended for planting in areas where the disease is not yet established.
